title: CORPS OF DISCOVERY
subtitle: St. Louis to the Pacific, 1804–1806
introBody: Spring, 1804. St. Louis, Missouri. President Jefferson has charged you to find a water route to the Pacific and map the unknown West. Your choices of supplies, crew, and pace will determine whether the Corps of Discovery reaches the ocean.
trailFeedOpener: May 1804: the keelboat pushes off from Camp Dubois into the Missouri River current.

events.title: Mandan Village
events.text: You reach the Mandan villages near present-day North Dakota. The Mandan people are skilled traders who can share knowledge of the land ahead. How you treat them will shape the rest of the journey.
trivia: The Corps spent the winter of 1804–1805 at Fort Mandan, built near a Mandan village.
Mandan people taught the Corps about the land and river routes ahead.

sageAdvice.name: Sacagawea
sageAdvice.line: Respect earns more than any trade goods.

sageAdvice.name: Pvt. Ordway
sageAdvice.line: Their food kept us alive through the winter.

choices.text: Trade fairly. Share gifts and listen.
choices.result: The Mandan welcome you warmly. You winter here, gathering maps and a new guide.
A polite but cold exchange. You save supplies but learn little.
A dangerous mistake. Without Mandan knowledge, the next leg goes poorly.

events.title: Great Falls Portage
events.text: The Missouri River falls in a series of five waterfalls. You must carry all boats and gear eighteen miles overland. This will take weeks and exhaust the crew.
events.imageSearchQuery: Great Falls Missouri River Lewis Clark 1805
trivia: The Great Falls portage took nearly a month and was one of the hardest parts of the journey.
Lewis and Clark built crude wagons from cottonwood to haul the heavy boats overland.

choices.result: Three brutal weeks. The crew builds wagon-wheels from cottonwood and hauls everything over. They make it.

outcomes.result: You bury supplies and mark the cache. Most items survive for the return trip.
Flooding ruins half the cached ammunition. A costly gamble.

choices.result: Grizzlies, cactus, and heat punish the crew. You finish, but barely.

image.searchQuery: Great Falls Missouri River Lewis Clark 1805 painting

events.title: Shoshone Nation
events.text: Sacagawea recognizes her homeland. The Shoshone chief is her brother. You desperately need horses to cross the Rocky Mountains — without them the expedition cannot continue.
trivia: Sacagawea's reunion with her Shoshone brother helped Lewis and Clark buy the horses they needed.
Without Shoshone horses, the Corps could not have crossed the Rocky Mountains.

sageAdvice.name: Sacagawea
sageAdvice.line: My people know these mountains. Listen to them.

choices.result: Sacagawea helps negotiate. You receive twenty-nine horses and a guide through the mountains.

outcomes.result: You get horses, but fewer than needed. The mountain crossing will be harder.
The Shoshone drive a hard bargain. Too few horses for a safe crossing.

choices.result: The Shoshone refuse. Without horses, you face the mountains on foot in approaching winter.

events.title: Bitterroot Crossing
events.text: The Bitterroot Mountains are brutal. Snow, steep trails, and near-starvation threaten the entire Corps. This is the most dangerous stretch of the entire expedition.
trivia: The Corps nearly starved in the Bitterroots in September 1805.
The Nez Perce people helped the Corps survive by providing food after the mountain crossing.

outcomes.result: Eleven miserable days. Horses and men survive on candles and bear grease. You make it through.
Two horses fall on the icy trail. Rations nearly gone. You emerge frostbitten.

choices.text: Push through fast. Beat the snow.
choices.result: You race winter and barely survive. Three horses lost, several men ill.

choices.text: Seek a Nez Perce guide first.
choices.result: Old Toby, a Nez Perce guide, leads you through. Slower, but far safer.

events.title: Pacific in Sight
events.text: The Pacific Ocean is close. Fog and rain soak the final miles. Each push through the coastal rainforest risks the crew's health but brings glory closer.

attempts.buttonText: Push through the fog to the shore
attempts.successText: You break through the treeline. The Pacific stretches to the horizon. The crew erupts in cheers.
attempts.failureText: Dense fog and soaked gear slow everything. Two men fall ill in the rain.

attempts.buttonText: Find high ground for a clear view
attempts.successText: From the ridge you see the full Pacific coastline. Lewis carves his name in a pine tree.
attempts.failureText: Rain and mud make the climb treacherous. A man twists his ankle badly.

attempts.buttonText: Wade into the surf — all the way in
attempts.successText: The Corps stands in the Pacific surf, shouting. Clark marks the date on a nearby tree: Nov. 18, 1805.
attempts.failureText: The surf is brutal. Men are knocked down by waves, gear soaked, ammunition ruined.

sages.name: President Thomas Jefferson
sages.title: President of the United States
sages.bio: Thomas Jefferson purchased the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803, doubling the size of the United States. He commissioned Lewis and Clark to explore this vast new land, find a route to the Pacific, and document the land, people, plants, and animals they encountered.
sages.greeting: Before you depart St. Louis, a letter arrives from Washington. President Jefferson outlines the mission's true scope in careful detail.
sages.advice: "You are to explore the Missouri River and reach the Pacific Ocean. Document everything — geography, plants, animals, and peoples. Establish peaceful relations with Native nations. This knowledge will serve the republic for generations."

question.question: Why did President Jefferson send Lewis and Clark west in 1804?
choices: To find gold and silver for the U.S. Treasury
To explore the Louisiana Purchase and find a route to the Pacific
To build forts and claim California from Spain
To relocate Native peoples to lands east of the Mississippi
question.explanation: After the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, Jefferson wanted the new territory explored and documented. He also hoped Lewis and Clark would find an all-water route to the Pacific to open trade.
question.teksRef: TEKS 5.1(A) — Historical significance of the Lewis and Clark Expedition

sages.name: Sacagawea
sages.title: Shoshone Interpreter & Guide
sages.bio: Sacagawea was a Shoshone woman who joined the expedition at Fort Mandan with her husband Toussaint Charbonneau. Her ability to speak Shoshone and identify plants, her knowledge of western geography, and her presence as a symbol of peace made her essential to the expedition's success.
sages.greeting: Near the headwaters of the Missouri, Sacagawea pauses and studies the horizon. She turns and speaks quietly.
sages.advice: "I know this land. The river bends here — my people camp beyond that ridge every summer. Trust what the land tells you, not only your maps."

question.question: Why was Sacagawea important to the Lewis and Clark Expedition?
choices: She drew all the official maps used by the Corps
She served as an interpreter and helped establish trust with Native nations
She commanded the keelboat through the Missouri rapids
She was sent by the U.S. Army as a military scout
question.explanation: Sacagawea spoke Shoshone and helped communicate with Native peoples. Her presence, especially with her infant son, signaled peaceful intentions. She also identified landmarks and helped obtain the horses the Corps needed.
question.teksRef: TEKS 5.1(B) — Lewis and Clark's interactions with Native peoples

sages.name: William Clark
sages.title: Co-Commander, Corps of Discovery
sages.bio: William Clark served as co-commander of the expedition alongside Meriwether Lewis. An experienced frontiersman and mapmaker, Clark produced detailed maps of the western lands the Corps traveled through — maps that would guide American settlers westward for decades.
sages.greeting: Clark spreads his latest map across a flat rock near the Columbia River and runs his finger along the route you've traveled.
sages.advice: "Every river, every ridge we mapped opens this country to those who come after. What we record here will outlast us both."

question.question: How did the Lewis and Clark Expedition support U.S. westward expansion?
choices: It built railroads through the Rocky Mountains
It mapped routes and lands that later settlers used to move west
It defeated Native armies and cleared the land for settlement
It established permanent U.S. forts all the way to the Pacific
question.explanation: Lewis and Clark produced detailed maps and journals describing western geography, resources, and peoples. These records guided future explorers, traders, and settlers and supported the United States' claim to western territories.
question.teksRef: TEKS 5.1(A) — Role of Lewis and Clark Expedition in westward expansion

eventTrivia.question: What did the United States gain from the Louisiana Purchase in 1803?
choices: A port in New Orleans only
A vast territory that doubled the size of the U.S.
The states of California and Oregon
eventTrivia.fact: The Louisiana Purchase bought roughly 828,000 square miles from France, doubling U.S. territory and opening the West to exploration.

eventTrivia.question: Why was goodwill with Native nations important to the Corps of Discovery?
choices: Native nations charged tolls on all rivers
Native peoples provided food, horses, knowledge, and safe passage
Congress required the Corps to trade furs with every tribe
eventTrivia.fact: Without help from the Mandan, Shoshone, and Nez Perce peoples — food, horses, and guides — the expedition could not have survived.

eventTrivia.question: What was one major result of the Lewis and Clark Expedition?
choices: The U.S. immediately built a railroad to the Pacific
Detailed maps and journals that encouraged future westward settlement
Spain gave up all claims to North America
eventTrivia.fact: Lewis and Clark's journals and maps gave Americans their first detailed picture of the West, supporting decades of westward expansion and settlement.

historicalContext: The Lewis and Clark Expedition of 1804–1806 was the first American overland expedition to reach the Pacific coast. Commissioned by President Jefferson after the Louisiana Purchase, the Corps of Discovery traveled over 8,000 miles round-trip, documented hundreds of new plant and animal species, produced detailed maps of the West, and established contacts with dozens of Native nations. Their journals became the foundation for American westward expansion in the 19th century.
